case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the government may treat a returning lawful permanent resident as an applicant for admission—and thus removable as inadmissible—based on proof developed after border processing (including later conviction evidence), rather than proving at the time of entry that the LPR falls within an exception in 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(13)(C).
case_analysis.legal_provision: Immigration and Nationality Act: 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(13)(C) (when a returning LPR is treated as seeking admission), 8 U.S.C. § 1182(a)(2) (criminal grounds of inadmissibility, including CIMTs), 8 U.S.C. § 1227 (grounds of deportability), 8 U.S.C. § 1229a(c)(3) (burden to prove removability), and INA § 212(h), 8 U.S.C. § 1182(h) (waiver of inadmissibility) (raised in the proceedings below).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The Attorney General argues that the Second Circuit incorrectly required the government to establish—at the moment of border inspection—by a heightened evidentiary showing that the returning LPR falls within a § 1101(a)(13)(C) exception (here, having 'committed' an offense described in § 1182(a)(2)). The government contends that Congress’s admission framework is conduct-based and would be unworkable if DHS had to meet conviction-level proof at the border; DHS may parole the LPR for further inspection and then rely on evidence that develops afterward (including criminal dispositions/convictions) to prove that an exception applied and that the individual is removable as inadmissible. The government also maintains that parole is not an admission and that the lawful/nonlawful character of parole should not bar removability once the removability showing is made in removal proceedings.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Lau argues that § 1101(a)(13)(C) is a protective rule for returning LPRs and that DHS must determine at the border, based on evidence available then, whether an exception applies before stripping the LPR of the statutory right to be treated as not seeking admission. He contends the government cannot bootstrap later-developed evidence (including a later conviction) to retroactively justify treating him as an applicant for admission at the time of entry. He further argues the government forfeited any challenge to the applicable burden of proof because it assumed below that a clear-and-convincing standard applies, and that the case is a poor vehicle because removability ultimately turns on whether his trademark-counterfeiting offense qualifies as a crime involving moral turpitude (CIMT), an issue the government did not ask the Court to decide. Respondent also suggests parole decisions may be reviewable as legal questions, though the government disputes reviewability.
key_precedents: Doe v. Attorney General of the United States, 659 F.3d 266 (3d Cir. 2011) (referenced regarding burden/standard for § 1101(a)(13)(C) exceptions)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s settled-expectations concern is the hardest point: if DHS can parole an LPR and later rely on newly assembled proof, it can look like post hoc recharacterization of the border encounter. But as Justice Kagan explains, § 1101(a)(13)(C) is framed as a substantive classification (“shall not be regarded … unless” a condition in fact exists), not a procedural timing rule that freezes what may be used to prove that condition, and Congress elsewhere chose § 1229a proceedings—with the Government’s burden under § 1229a(c)(3)—as the forum for definitive proof. Properly understood, later-developed evidence (including a conviction record) is evidence of an antecedent fact—whether the LPR “has committed” the § 1182(a)(2) offense as of reentry—rather than a retroactive change in legal status; parole is not an admission, so there is no statutory “lock-in” that fairness can supply without adding words to the statute. Consistent with judicial minimalism, I would adopt a narrow holding limited to the permissibility of relying on evidence developed in removal proceedings to prove an exception under § 1101(a)(13)(C), without opining more broadly on the underlying offense classification beyond what is necessary.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point—that allowing later-developed proof “recharacterizes” the entry and defeats settled expectations—cannot justify adding a border-time evidentiary cutoff that Congress did not write into § 1101(a)(13)(C). As the Chief Justice notes, the text sets a substantive condition (the LPR “has committed” a § 1182(a)(2) offense) and the INA’s structure assigns the definitive, burdened adjudication to § 1229a removal proceedings, not to a port-of-entry mini-trial. The later conviction record is not retroactive status-making; it is evidence of an antecedent fact that either existed at reentry or did not, and parole/further inspection is not an “admission” that could estop the Government from proving the statutory exception later. Whatever the equities, reinstating a Fleuti-like, judge-made timing rule would be atextual and inconsistent with IIRIRA’s enumerated framework, as Justice Gorsuch and Justice Kagan emphasize.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is the fairness/settled-expectations concern that DHS can “recharacterize” the entry later, but that argument depends on reading § 1101(a)(13)(C) as imposing an at-the-border evidentiary deadline that the text does not contain. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Congress set a substantive trigger—whether the LPR “has committed” a § 1182(a)(2) offense—and the INA’s structure channels the definitive proof and burden to § 1229a proceedings, where the Government must establish removability on a full record. Treating later-obtained conviction records as proof of an antecedent fact is not retroactive rewriting; it avoids creating an atextual safe harbor keyed to what can be proven at inspection and preserves IIRIRA’s administrable design separating screening from adjudication. Fairness concerns are answered by the procedural protections of the removal hearing rather than by grafting a timing cutoff onto § 1101(a)(13)(C).

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan are right that § 1101(a)(13)(C) lacks an express "at-the-booth" evidentiary deadline and that § 1229a(c)(3) channels proof questions into removal proceedings, but that structural point does not resolve the antecedent statutory allocation in § 1101(a)(13)(C): whether the returning LPR is to be treated as an applicant for admission at all based on what the Government chooses (and can justify) at the border encounter. Allowing DHS to parole or admit an LPR without invoking an exception, and then later—based on subsequently crystallized proof like a later conviction—recast that same return as an "application for admission" risks turning Congress’s protective default (“shall not be regarded”) into a revocable label, undermining notice and settled expectations for long-term residents. Justice Alito’s administrability concerns are real, but IIRIRA’s move from Fleuti to enumerated exceptions does not imply Congress also authorized after-the-fact bootstrapping that expands detention/removal exposure without a timely, contestable classification decision at reentry. Vartelas, as invoked by several colleagues, reinforces that IIRIRA drew specific lines for when travel triggers admission consequences; it does not suggest those lines can be enforced by retroactively recharacterizing the legal nature of an entry once the Government later assembles better evidence.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s notice/settled-expectations concern is serious, but it reads a timing-and-proof limitation into § 1101(a)(13)(C) that the text does not supply; the clause operates as a substantive classification (“shall not be regarded … unless” a condition exists), not an instruction to freeze the evidentiary record at inspection. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett stress, the INA’s structure places the dispositive adjudication and burden in § 1229a removal proceedings, making it implausible that Congress silently required DHS to litigate the “has committed” question conclusively at the port of entry. The feared “post hoc recharacterization” is better understood as later-developed evidence proving an antecedent fact that existed at reentry, with procedural protections supplied by the adversarial hearing and the Government’s burden there. Vartelas, as several colleagues note, underscores that IIRIRA replaced Fleuti with an administrable trigger list—not that Congress created an atextual border-time evidentiary lock-in.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s fairness/notice objection is the best counter, but it asks us to graft onto § 1101(a)(13)(C) an atextual, at-the-booth evidentiary cutoff: the statute turns on whether the LPR “has committed” a covered offense, not whether DHS can prove it instantly at inspection. As the Chief Justice emphasizes, the INA’s structure channels definitive determinations—and the Government’s burden—into § 1229a removal proceedings, which is where Congress contemplated contested proof would be tested; later-developed evidence is simply evidence of an antecedent fact, not a retroactive change in legal status. To adopt Sotomayor’s rule would recreate, in another guise, the sort of judge-made overlay IIRIRA displaced when it replaced Fleuti with enumerated exceptions. Vartelas confirms that Congress drew the operative lines in § 1101(a)(13)(C); it does not authorize us to add an implied timing rule in the name of equity.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s fairness/settled-expectations concern is the best argument for Respondent, but it depends on reading “shall not be regarded as seeking an admission unless” as an at-the-border evidentiary cutoff; the text instead sets a substantive condition (e.g., the LPR “has committed” a § 1182(a)(2) offense) without prescribing when or how DHS must prove it. Chief Justice Roberts’s structural point is persuasive: Congress located the dispositive adjudication and burden in § 1229a proceedings, so allowing conviction records developed later to prove the preexisting fact of “has committed” fits the INA’s design and preserves due process through an adversarial hearing. Vartelas’s discussion of IIRIRA displacing Fleuti reinforces, for me, that we should not graft a judicially created timing rule onto § 1101(a)(13)(C) in the name of equity—especially where parole is not an admission and later proof does not retroactively change the legal character of the entry so much as establish an antecedent statutory trigger. Practical administrability concerns noted by Justice Alito further counsel against inventing a port-of-entry mini-trial requirement absent clear statutory direction.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s fairness/settled-expectations concern remains the most serious counter, but it depends on reading § 1101(a)(13)(C)’s “shall not be regarded … unless” as an implied border-time evidentiary lock-in that the text does not supply. As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, the INA’s structure assigns the ultimate determination and burdens of proof to § 1229a proceedings, making it unsurprising that conclusive proof (including conviction records) may crystallize there rather than at the booth. Later-developed evidence does not retroactively change the legal character of the encounter; it proves an antecedent fact—whether the LPR “has committed” a § 1182(a)(2) offense—which is a substantive condition that either existed at reentry or did not. Under an originalist/textualist approach, I do not see a basis to graft an atextual timing requirement onto Congress’s enumerated IIRIRA framework, particularly given parole’s distinct statutory role.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is the notice/settled-expectations concern that DHS can “recharacterize” a return after the fact, but I don’t see a textual foothold for turning § 1101(a)(13)(C)’s substantive “unless” conditions into an at-the-booth evidentiary cutoff. As Justice Kagan and the Chief emphasize, the INA’s design channels the decisive determination—and the Government’s burden—into § 1229a proceedings, which are more procedurally protective than port-of-entry screening and better suited to testing whether the LPR in fact “has committed” a § 1182(a)(2) offense as of reentry. Under my pragmatic, process-focused approach, allowing later-developed proof does not retroactively change the legal status of the entry; it supplies evidence about an antecedent fact while preserving the LPR’s opportunity to contest removability in an adversarial forum. Vartelas’s discussion of IIRIRA replacing Fleuti underscores Congress’s move to administrable, enumerated triggers, not a judicially created timing rule that would invite arbitrary outcomes keyed to what can be proven in secondary inspection.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 1101(a)(13)(C) sets out the substantive exceptions under which a returning LPR is treated as seeking admission, but it does not prescribe a time-of-entry evidentiary lock-in that would bar DHS from relying on proof developed in subsequent removal proceedings to show an exception applied. The INA’s structure places the operative “clear and convincing” burden for removability in removal proceedings, see 8 U.S.C. § 1229a(c)(3), and nothing in § 1101(a)(13)(C) shifts that burden to the initial inspection process or forbids later-developed evidence (including a conviction) from establishing the relevant “has committed” § 1182(a)(2) conduct. Congress’s IIRIRA amendments partially codified and partially abrogated Fleuti’s protective rule to restore meaningful border scrutiny of returning LPRs, consistent with permitting parole for further inspection and later proof without converting parole into an admission. A narrow reversal on this statutory, procedural ground best preserves administrable border rules and institutional legitimacy while leaving open any unresolved merits questions (e.g., whether the offense is a CIMT).

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(13)(C) establishes a status rule—an LPR “shall not be regarded as seeking an admission … unless” one of the enumerated conditions exists—but it does not impose a temporal-evidence limitation requiring DHS to prove the exception “at the moment” of border inspection. Section 1101(a)(13)(C)(v) turns on whether the LPR “has committed an offense identified in section 1182(a)(2),” a conduct-based predicate that may be established in subsequent removal proceedings under § 1229a(c)(3), which governs the proof of removability, including through later-developed evidence such as conviction records. Congress in IIRIRA replaced Fleuti’s judicial doctrine with this enumerated framework to restore meaningful border scrutiny for returning LPRs, and nothing in the statutory text converts parole or further inspection into an “admission” that would foreclose later reliance on admissibility grounds. Because the Second Circuit’s rule adds atextual constraints and frustrates Congress’s 1996 design, I would reverse.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The text of 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(13)(C) asks whether the returning LPR "has committed" an offense described in § 1182(a)(2), and nothing in that provision imposes a timing rule requiring DHS to prove the exception conclusively at the instant of border inspection rather than in later removal proceedings governed by § 1229a(c)(3). Reading in an at-the-border evidentiary cutoff would be atextual and would frustrate Congress’s IIRIRA design to restore meaningful border scrutiny after Rosenberg v. Fleuti by allowing parole for further inspection and then litigating admissibility based on the full record, including later-developed conviction evidence relevant to whether the alien in fact committed a § 1182(a)(2) offense. Practical consequences also matter: requiring conviction-level proof at the border would be unworkable and would impair enforcement against returning residents whose criminal conduct is not immediately verifiable at primary/secondary inspection. Because parole is not an admission, later proof in removal proceedings can establish that the LPR properly falls within § 1101(a)(13)(C) and is removable as inadmissible under § 1182(a)(2).

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 1101(a)(13)(C) is a protective rule that preserves the baseline that a returning lawful permanent resident “shall not be regarded as seeking an admission” unless DHS establishes, at the time of the attempted reentry, that one of the enumerated exceptions applies; allowing the government to rely on later-developed proof (including a later conviction) effectively nullifies that protection and invites retroactive recharacterization of a lawful return. Congress narrowed Fleuti with IIRIRA, but it did so through a specified, cabined list of exceptions in § 1101(a)(13)(C), not by authorizing post hoc bootstrapping that erodes settled expectations and access to fair process for long-term residents. The INA’s structure reinforces that allocation: the government bears the burden to prove removability in removal proceedings, 8 U.S.C. § 1229a(c)(3), and the “committed” language in § 1101(a)(13)(C)(v) cannot be read to permit stripping LPR status based on evidence that did not exist (or was not established) when DHS made the admission-versus-parole choice at the border. Practical consequences confirm the point—permitting after-the-fact justification expands detention and removal risk for LPRs without timely notice or meaningful ability to contest the triggering facts at entry, undermining fairness for a particularly vulnerable population.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 1101(a)(13)(C) sets a substantive condition for when a returning LPR is “seeking admission,” but it does not prescribe that DHS must finally prove the triggering facts at the instant of border inspection; removal proceedings under § 1229a are the designed forum for adjudicating removability, with the government bearing the burden to prove inadmissibility/deportability as applicable. Reading § 1101(a)(13)(C) to require conviction-level proof at the border would be textually unmoored and practically unworkable, given that Congress separately authorizes parole for “alien[s] applying for admission” in § 1182(d)(5)(A) and contemplates further process before the ultimate removability determination. Consistent with circuits allowing the use of later-developed conviction evidence to establish that the § 1101(a)(13)(C)(v) exception applied (and thus that inadmissibility grounds in § 1182(a)(2) may be charged), the statute is best read to permit DHS to parole for further inspection and then meet its burden in removal proceedings with the complete record. Fleuti’s prior, more protective “innocent, casual, and brief excursion” doctrine was displaced by IIRIRA’s codification/abrogation in § 1101(a)(13)(C), which favors a clear, workable admissions framework rather than a timing rule that would turn on what could be proven at the booth.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 1101(a)(13)(C) asks whether a returning LPR “has committed” an offense described in § 1182(a)(2); nothing in that text requires DHS to conclusively prove the exception at the port of entry or forbids establishing the relevant facts later in § 1229a removal proceedings, where the government bears the burden to prove removability. Reading the statute to impose an at-the-border evidentiary fixation would add words Congress did not write and would sit uneasily with Congress’s 1996 replacement of Fleuti’s judge-made, trip-focused approach with a rule restoring meaningful inspection and allowing specified categories of returning LPRs to be treated as applicants for admission. The better textual reading is that the exception turns on the alien’s status and past conduct as of reentry, but proof of those facts may be developed and tested in removal proceedings; parole does not itself constitute an “admission” and does not bar an inadmissibility-based charge once removability is shown. To the extent any ambiguity remains about when and how proof may be adduced, the statute supplies no basis for a special border-time evidentiary requirement, and the separation-of-powers role of this Court is to apply the enacted text rather than resurrecting a Fleuti-like judicial gloss.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 1101(a)(13)(C) sets a substantive rule about when a returning LPR “shall not be regarded as seeking an admission” unless one of the listed exceptions applies, but it does not specify that DHS must finally prove the exception at primary inspection or forever lose the ability to proceed under § 1182 in later removal proceedings. Given IIRIRA’s partial abrogation of Fleuti and Congress’s evident aim to restore meaningful border scrutiny for LPRs with criminal conduct, it is more consistent with the statutory structure to allow the Government to parole for further inspection and then satisfy its burden in § 1229a proceedings using reliable later-developed proof (including conviction records) that the alien had “committed” an offense described in § 1182(a)(2). A rigid “at-the-border, evidence-on-hand only” rule is not textually compelled and would be practically unworkable, while still preserving due process because removability must ultimately be established in the removal hearing under the applicable burden in § 1229a(c)(3). This approach accords with judicial restraint and administrability and avoids extending Fleuti beyond what Congress codified in § 1101(a)(13)(C).

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The text of 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(13)(C) asks whether the returning LPR “has committed” one of the listed acts, a conduct-based inquiry that does not on its face impose a contemporaneous-at-the-port evidentiary limitation or bar the government from proving the exception in later removal proceedings. Reading § 1101(a)(13)(C) alongside § 1229a(c)(3) (government’s burden to prove removability in proceedings) and § 1225(a)(1) (arriving aliens deemed applicants for admission, subject to the LPR carveout), the more methodologically consistent approach is to treat the border encounter as initiating inspection/parole and to adjudicate—on a full record—whether an exception applied, rather than freezing proof at the moment of inspection. Congress in IIRIRA replaced the Fleuti “entry” regime and specified limited circumstances when LPRs are treated as seeking admission, reflecting an intent to restore meaningful border scrutiny rather than create an evidentiary safe harbor keyed to what can be proven instantly at the port of entry. Precedent recognizing IIRIRA’s partial abrogation/codification of Fleuti, including Vartelas’s description of § 1101(a)(13)(C), supports that Congress set substantive triggers (e.g., criminal conduct) without prescribing an at-the-border proof rule.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 1101(a)(13)(C) identifies conduct-based circumstances in which a returning LPR “shall be regarded as seeking an admission,” and the INA’s structure channels the definitive proof of removability to removal proceedings, where the government bears the burden to prove inadmissibility by clear and convincing evidence. Reading § 1101(a)(13)(C) to require DHS to conclusively establish an exception at the port of entry based only on facts known then would improperly collapse the statute’s screening/adjudication framework, undermine Congress’s post-Fleuti reforms in IIRIRA, and create serious practical consequences for border administration. Consistent with that design, DHS may parole a returning LPR for further inspection and then rely on later-developed, reliable evidence (including convictions) in the ensuing § 1229a proceeding to prove that an exception applied and the LPR is removable as inadmissible under § 1182(a)(2). This approach preserves procedural fairness by ensuring the dispositive determination occurs in an adversarial hearing with judicial factfinding and a defined burden, rather than at the border in a summary setting.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the government may treat a returning lawful permanent resident as an applicant for admission based on proof developed after entry (e.g., later conviction records), rather than proving at the border that the resident had already “committed” an offense triggering an exception in 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(13)(C).
case_analysis.legal_provision: Immigration and Nationality Act: 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(13)(C) (returning LPRs and when they are treated as seeking admission), and related admissibility/removability provisions including 8 U.S.C. § 1182(a)(2) (criminal inadmissibility) and the burden concepts tied to 8 U.S.C. §§ 1182/1229a/1227; also implicated is discretionary parole authority (8 U.S.C. § 1182(d)(5)) and judicial review limits in 8 U.S.C. § 1252(a)(2)(B) (discussed at argument).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The government argues that the INA’s structure is conduct-based at the border and does not require ‘conviction-level’ proof at the moment of inspection to invoke a § 1101(a)(13)(C) exception; DHS can parole a returning LPR for further processing and later rely on information that becomes available (including post-parole documentation of pre-entry criminal conduct/conviction) to establish that an exception applied, allowing the government to proceed on the inadmissibility track.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent argues that § 1101(a)(13)(C) requires the government to justify, as of the time of inspection at the border, treating a returning LPR as seeking admission; the government cannot retroactively convert an LPR into an applicant for admission based on later-developed evidence, and the Second Circuit correctly required an at-the-border determination (with the burden on the government, and—respondent contends—properly clear and convincing evidence) before stripping the LPR of the presumption of admission as a returning resident.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Jackson and Justice Sotomayor press the best counterpoint: the “shall not be regarded … unless” phrasing sounds like a threshold, inspection-time gatekeeping rule, and they warn of a parole-first, protections-later maneuver. But as Justice Kagan explains, § 1101(a)(13)(C) is triggered by a historical predicate (“has committed” a § 1182(a)(2) offense), not by what proof DHS happens to have at the booth, and the INA’s structure sensibly separates screening at the border from adjudication in § 1229a where DHS must still prove the exception applied at the time of return. Vartelas, as Justice Alito notes, describes IIRIRA as narrowing Fleuti, which counsels against reading an extra-textual contemporaneous-proof requirement into Congress’s replacement scheme. A narrow holding can address fairness by making clear the government bears the burden in removal proceedings to show the § 1101(a)(13)(C) exception in fact existed at reentry, while rejecting a rigid inspection-time evidentiary rule.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson’s best point is that § 1101(a)(13)(C)’s “shall not be regarded … unless” sounds like a threshold, inspection-time classification and that post hoc proof risks parole-first manipulation. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan explain, the statute’s operative triggers are factual predicates—especially that the LPR “has committed” a § 1182(a)(2) offense—and the text contains no timing-of-proof requirement that DHS must conclusively establish the exception at the booth rather than in § 1229a proceedings. Under a textualist, original-public-meaning approach, we cannot add an atextual evidentiary checkpoint to preserve a fairness buffer akin to Fleuti; Vartelas’s discussion of IIRIRA’s narrowing of Fleuti confirms Congress chose a conduct-based rule, not a documentation-at-inspection rule. Because parole under § 1182(d)(5) is not an admission, allowing DHS to parole for further processing and later prove the exception applied at the time of return is not “retroactive conversion,” but later adjudication of an earlier-existing fact.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Jackson and Justice Sotomayor’s “retroactive reclassification” and parole-first concerns are serious as a policy matter, but they do not overcome the statutory text, which turns on whether the LPR in fact “has committed” a § 1182(a)(2) offense—not on whether DHS can prove that fact at primary inspection. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, the INA’s structure sensibly treats inspection as screening and § 1229a proceedings as adjudication, where the Government must still carry its burden to show the § 1101(a)(13)(C) exception actually applied at the time of return. Parole under § 1182(d)(5) does not itself effect an “admission,” so allowing parole for further processing does not collapse categories; it preserves administrability without immunizing the Government from later proof obligations. Vartelas, as Justice Thomas notes, confirms Congress narrowed Fleuti-like insulation, and I see no textual basis to reintroduce an extra-statutory timing-of-proof requirement.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s best point is that § 1101(a)(13)(C) uses fact predicates (“has committed”) and does not expressly time-lock the government’s proof to primary inspection, with ultimate proof supplied in § 1229a proceedings. But the operative command—an LPR “shall not be regarded as seeking an admission unless”—is a threshold classification that determines which legal regime (inadmissibility vs. post-admission removability) and which burdens attach, and under my pragmatic approach that gatekeeping protection is hollow if DHS can parole first and only later justify having treated the person as an applicant for admission. Vartelas confirms IIRIRA narrowed Fleuti’s substantive “brief, casual, innocent” protection, but it does not answer this distinct procedural timing question, and I am not persuaded that Congress clearly authorized retroactive conversion of returning-resident status through post-entry evidence development. Administrability concerns Justice Kagan raises are real, yet they can be addressed by requiring DHS to meet a threshold showing before invoking the admission track, rather than shifting the risk of uncertainty onto long-term residents.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Jackson and Justice Sotomayor make the best fairness/structure point: the “shall not be regarded … unless” formulation sounds like a gatekeeping classification that, if postponed, could enable a parole-first, consequences-later play. But on a pragmatic textualist read, the statute’s triggers are fact predicates (“has committed” an offense), not an instruction about what DHS must be able to prove at the inspection booth, and importing a contemporaneous-proof requirement would add procedural machinery Congress did not write. Chief Justice Roberts’s structural observation that the INA separates screening/parole under § 1182(d)(5) from adjudication in § 1229a proceedings strengthens the coherent, workable interpretation: DHS may parole for processing, but must later prove that an exception actually applied at the time of return to use the inadmissibility track. Vartelas (as Justice Alito notes) confirms IIRIRA narrowed judge-made insulation like Fleuti; that cautions against creating a new, extra-textual “prove-it-at-the-booth” constraint as the mechanism for protecting returning LPRs.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Jackson’s and Justice Sotomayor’s best point is that “shall not be regarded as seeking an admission unless” sounds like a threshold, inspection-time protection, and that parole could be used to game the system. But the statutory exception turns on a historical fact—whether the LPR “has committed” a § 1182(a)(2) offense—rather than on what evidence DHS has assembled at the booth, and I do not see any textual hook for an atextual timing-of-proof requirement. As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, the INA’s structure expects disputed admissibility predicates to be adjudicated in § 1229a proceedings after parole for processing, with DHS still bearing the burden to prove that the § 1101(a)(13)(C) exception applied at the moment of return—so this is not “retroactive conversion,” just later proof of an earlier-existing status. Vartelas, as Justice Alito notes, underscores that IIRIRA narrowed Fleuti’s judge-made protections, and I am not prepared to recreate a new, judge-made prophylactic rule untethered to the enacted text.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Jackson’s and Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point—that § 1101(a)(13)(C)’s “shall not be regarded … unless” creates an inspection-time procedural protection that is defeated by later proof—has force as a fairness and anti-gamesmanship concern. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan explain, the statutory triggers are framed as historical, conduct-based predicates (“has committed”), not as an evidentiary timing rule, and nothing in the text says DHS must possess conviction-grade proof at primary inspection before using congressionally authorized parole to complete processing and then litigate the classification in § 1229a. Vartelas (as Justice Alito notes) reinforces that IIRIRA replaced Fleuti’s extra-textual insulation with Congress’s specified exceptions; importing a “prove-it-at-the-booth” requirement would recreate a protective buffer Congress did not write and would, in practice, collapse screening into adjudication. On an institutionalist, precedent-and-structure approach, the better reading is that removal proceedings determine whether the exception in fact applied at the time of return, with DHS still bearing the burden there, which mitigates the parole-first concern without adding atextual constraints.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Jackson’s strongest point is that § 1101(a)(13)(C)’s “shall not be regarded as seeking an admission unless” operates as an inspection-time gatekeeping rule, and that allowing later-developed proof invites DHS “parole-first” maneuvering. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, the statute’s operative triggers—especially that the LPR “has committed” a § 1182(a)(2) offense—describe an objective historical fact, not the government’s evidentiary posture at the port of entry, and the text supplies no timing-of-proof requirement. The INA’s structure contemplates that parole under § 1182(d)(5) can facilitate completing inspection while disputed admissibility predicates are adjudicated later in § 1229a proceedings, with DHS still bearing the burden to prove the § 1101(a)(13)(C) exception applied at the time of return. Vartelas’s account of IIRIRA as narrowing Fleuti supports reading § 1101(a)(13)(C) as Congress’s substantive line for when an LPR is properly treated as seeking admission, not as freezing that determination to whatever documentation happens to be available at primary inspection.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: I take Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s central point seriously: § 1101(a)(13)(C) is written in conduct terms (“has committed”) and does not expressly require DHS to possess conclusive proof at the inspection booth. But the operative structure—an LPR “shall not be regarded as seeking an admission unless” DHS can invoke an exception—functions as a gatekeeping rule for the government’s choice of procedural track at the border, and allowing DHS to parole first and later supply the predicate risks converting that threshold protection into a post hoc consequences regime that undermines procedural fairness for returning long-term residents. Justice Alito’s administrability concern does not persuade me because Congress already supplied workable alternatives (including admitting the LPR and proceeding under § 1227), and parole-plus-retroactive-reclassification predictably invites incentives that dilute the statutory presumption in favor of LPRs at reentry. Vartelas confirms IIRIRA narrowed Fleuti’s substantive test, but it does not resolve this distinct timing/procedure question; on pragmatic grounds, the best reading ties DHS’s “unless” showing to the initial decision to treat the LPR as an applicant for admission rather than letting that classification crystallize later.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 1101(a)(13)(C) sets the substantive conditions under which a returning LPR “shall not be regarded as seeking an admission unless” an enumerated exception applies, but it does not clearly require that the government possess or marshal conviction-level proof at the moment of inspection, as opposed to establishing in later § 1229a proceedings that the exception in fact applied at return. Treating the question as one of ultimate classification for the removal case—rather than a rigid at-the-border evidentiary checkpoint—fits the INA’s structure (including DHS’s ability to parole for further processing under § 1182(d)(5)) while preserving institutional administrability and avoiding a sweeping rule about parole reviewability under § 1252(a)(2)(B). I would reverse the Second Circuit’s at-the-border proof requirement and hold narrowly that later-developed evidence may be used in removal proceedings to prove a § 1101(a)(13)(C) exception applied when the LPR sought reentry, leaving the precise burden/standard to the agency in the first instance. This reading remains consistent with Fleuti’s post-IIRIRA codification: § 1101(a)(13)(C) defines when an LPR is treated as seeking admission, but does not constitutionalize or time-lock the evidentiary showing to the inspection moment.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(13)(C) asks whether a returning LPR “has committed” an offense described in § 1182(a)(2), and nothing in that language requires the Government to possess conviction-level proof at the moment of inspection rather than establishing the predicate facts in later proceedings. Reading an “at-the-border proof” requirement into § 1101(a)(13)(C) would add words Congress did not enact and would reintroduce a Fleuti-like insulation from meaningful border scrutiny that IIRIRA was designed to curtail by replacing “entry” with “admission” and enumerating specific exceptions for returning LPRs. So long as DHS proceeds under the statute Congress wrote—and proves in removal proceedings that an exception in § 1101(a)(13)(C) applied—the Government may rely on evidence developed after parole/entry to meet that burden. Rosenberg v. Fleuti underscores the point: Congress in 1996 narrowed that judge-made doctrine through § 1101(a)(13)(C), and courts should not recreate it by imposing extra-textual timing and evidentiary requirements.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 1101(a)(13)(C) provides that a returning lawful permanent resident “shall not be regarded as seeking an admission … unless” one of the enumerated exceptions applies, but it does not impose a timing requirement that the Government must definitively prove the exception’s factual predicates at the port of entry. Given the INA’s structure—especially DHS’s express parole authority in § 1182(d)(5) and the inspection framework in § 1225(a)(1)—it is consistent with the statutory text and practical border realities to allow DHS to parole an LPR for further processing and later, in removal proceedings, establish that § 1101(a)(13)(C)(v) applied (e.g., that the alien “has committed” a § 1182(a)(2) offense). Requiring “conviction-level” proof at the border would hamstring inspection, invite gamesmanship, and undermine law-enforcement interests without any clear textual command. Vartelas recognizes that IIRIRA’s 1996 enactment of § 1101(a)(13)(C) adjusted (and in part abrogated) Fleuti’s more forgiving rule, supporting a reading that permits the Government to apply the statutory exceptions in a workable, enforcement-oriented manner rather than freezing admissibility classification based solely on what paperwork happens to be in hand at the moment of inspection.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 1101(a)(13)(C) sets a threshold, inspection-time limitation on when a returning lawful permanent resident may be treated as “seeking an admission,” and the government cannot retroactively reclassify an LPR based on proof assembled after entry and parole; the statute’s present-tense, status-defining structure (“shall not be regarded as seeking an admission unless”) points to a determination tied to the time of inspection, not later litigation strategy. Congress’s 1996 response to Rosenberg v. Fleuti narrowed—but did not erase—the returning-resident presumption, and reading § 1101(a)(13)(C) to permit post-entry proof to trigger inadmissibility would let DHS bypass the more protective post-admission removal track in § 1227 simply by paroling first, a maneuver with serious fairness and access-to-justice consequences for long-term residents. Whatever DHS’s ability to investigate, the government must carry the burden to justify treating an LPR as an applicant for admission at the border under § 1101(a)(13)(C) before routing the case into § 1182(a)(2)’s inadmissibility regime; otherwise parole becomes a broad remedial workaround that undermines the statutory line Congress drew.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 1101(a)(13)(C) defines when a returning LPR “shall not be regarded as seeking an admission … unless” an enumerated condition applies, but it does not prescribe that DHS must conclusively prove that condition at primary inspection, as opposed to establishing it later in removal proceedings. Given Congress’s IIRIRA restructuring—separating inadmissibility (§ 1182) and removability while preserving parole authority (§ 1182(d)(5))—a workable reading allows DHS to parole for further processing and then carry its burden in proceedings to show that an exception in § 1101(a)(13)(C) applied at the time of return, using subsequently obtained conviction records as proof of pre-existing facts. That approach fits the text’s conduct-focused trigger (e.g., having “committed” an offense) and avoids an administrability problem in which border officers must litigate complex criminal-history questions on the spot, while still requiring the government to justify the track choice before the IJ. Fleuti’s “innocent, casual, and brief” doctrine was partially abrogated/codified by § 1101(a)(13)(C), and nothing in that codification compels a rigid “prove-it-at-the-booth” timing rule.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 1101(a)(13)(C) asks whether the returning LPR “has committed” a disqualifying offense, and nothing in that text imposes a timing-of-proof requirement that the Government possess conviction-level evidence at the moment of inspection; the Fifth Circuit’s reading in Munoz v. Holder is consistent with the statute’s ordinary meaning. Congress in IIRIRA replaced Fleuti’s judge-made “innocent, casual, and brief” test with a statutory set of exceptions, and it did not add an at-the-border evidentiary requirement—courts should not rewrite the statute to do so. The Second Circuit’s rule effectively constrains DHS’s ability to use parole under 8 U.S.C. § 1182(d)(5) to complete inspection and then, in removal proceedings under § 1229a, prove the § 1101(a)(13)(C) exception with the best available evidence, which better accords with the INA’s structure. Any residual ambiguity about evidentiary burdens at the threshold should not be resolved by agency deference, but here the plain statutory text does not support respondent’s retroactivity/at-the-border proof limitation.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 1101(a)(13)(C)(v) directs that a returning LPR “shall be regarded as seeking an admission” if he “has committed” an offense described in § 1182(a)(2), and that conduct-based phrasing does not require the government to possess conviction records or make a conclusive merits determination at the port of entry. Consistent with IIRIRA’s post-Fleuti framework, border inspection is a screening stage and contested admissibility issues are ordinarily resolved in § 1229a removal proceedings, where the government may rely on reliable evidence developed after entry; reading the statute to freeze proof at the moment of inspection would make parole under § 1182(d)(5) far less workable and collapse screening into adjudication. This interpretation also fits Congress’s 1996 partial abrogation of Fleuti by replacing a judge-made “brief, casual, and innocent” test with enumerated statutory exceptions that operate as jurisdictional gateways to the inadmissibility track. Nothing in the text of § 1101(a)(13)(C) imposes an at-the-border evidentiary burden of “clear and convincing,” a standard that appears to derive from BIA gloss rather than statutory command, and judicial restraint counsels against engrafting that requirement onto the statute.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 1101(a)(13)(C) is framed in conduct-based terms—an LPR “shall not be regarded as seeking an admission unless” one of six exceptions applies—and nothing in that text imposes a timing requirement that the government must possess conviction-level proof “at the border” to invoke an exception later in proceedings. The INA’s broader structure contemplates that admissibility determinations may be litigated in removal proceedings (e.g., 8 U.S.C. §§ 1225(a)(1), 1229a), and Congress’s IIRIRA revisions were meant to restore meaningful border scrutiny of returning LPRs rather than to create a categorical bar on using subsequently obtained evidence of pre-entry disqualifying conduct. Treating parole under § 1182(d)(5) as a mechanism to allow entry for further processing, while permitting DHS later to prove an exception applied, fits the statutory design without converting parole into an “admission.” Consistent with Vartelas’s description of § 1101(a)(13)(C) as partially codifying and partially abrogating Fleuti, the statute is best read to tie status to whether an exception in fact applied—not to what could be proven at the inspection booth at that moment.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 1101(a)(13)(C) sets a default rule that a returning lawful permanent resident “shall not be regarded as seeking an admission” unless DHS establishes, at the time of inspection, that one of the enumerated exceptions applies; reading the statute to permit a later, retroactive “conversion” based on post-entry proof (like later-obtained conviction records) dilutes that procedural protection and shifts the system from a threshold border determination to a consequences-later regime. Congress enacted § 1101(a)(13)(C) to partially codify and partially narrow Rosenberg v. Fleuti’s solicitude for returning LPRs, not to eliminate the requirement that the government justify treating an LPR as an applicant for admission when the government chooses the inadmissibility track under § 1182(a)(2) rather than removability under § 1227. The statute’s present-tense framing of several exceptions and the overall burden structure (distinct admission vs. removal pathways) support requiring DHS to carry its burden on the triggering exception contemporaneously, which better aligns with procedural fairness and avoids practical incentives to parole first and litigate admissibility later. Nothing in § 1182(d)(5) parole authority or § 1252(a)(2)(B) review limits supplies a clear authorization to bypass that threshold determination.
